```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE)
```

Summary of three svCapture replicates applied to TTF2 WT, degraded, and 
complemented HCT116. Two ways of plotting and two ways of assessing significance 
are shown due to known library batch effects, especially the third vs. the first 
and second replicates.

### Initialize

```{r}
library(data.table)
library(ggplot2)
library(MASS) # for glm.nb
```

### Load Data

svCapture data were processed by the published pipeline that is part of the 
[svx-mdi-tools](https://wilsontelab.github.io/svx-mdi-tools/docs/svCapture/00_svCapture.html)
GitHub repository. The assembly app was used to download the following CSV 
file, which is provided with this RMarkdown file, where:

* **project**	= name given to one of three batches of samples each processed together
* **coverage** = average read coverage in the _FHIT_ and _WWOX_ capture target regions,
                 used to normalize SV deletion counts
* **deletion** = number of _de novo_ singleton deletion SVs observed for a sample in the capture target regions
* other columns describe sample experimental attributes


```{r}
data <- fread("TTF2_data_121625.csv")
data[, project := factor(project)]
str(data)
data[1:5]
```

### Calculate SV Frequency Per Sample

The burden of deletion SVs in each sample, named 'SV Frequency', is calculated as
`deletion / coverage`, which intuitively correlates with the number of alleles 
in the sequenced DNA that had a detected _de novo_ singleton deletion SV. Deletion 
frequencies can be quite high with APH stress.

```{r}
data[, sample_group := factor(sample_label, levels = unique(sample_label))]
data[, sv_freq := deletion / coverage]
data[1:5, .(sample_group, deletion, coverage, sv_freq)]
```

### Calculate Mean SV Frequency Per Sample Type

Aggregate by sample attributes and calculate `mean(sv_freq)`.

```{r}
grouped_data <- data[, .(mean_sv_freq = mean(sv_freq)), keyby = .(sample_group)]
grouped_data[1:5]
```

### Plot Unnormalized SV Frequency

We typically plot data as SV Frequency without any additional normalization. 
The strong batch effect of 'HCT_Pellman_121125' vs. the others is apparent.

```{r}
ggplot() +
  geom_col(
    data = grouped_data,
    aes(x = sample_group, y = mean_sv_freq),
    fill = "grey80", color = "black", width = 0.7
  ) +
  geom_jitter(
    data = data,
    aes(x = sample_group, y = sv_freq, color = project),
    width = 0.15, height = 0, size = 2, alpha = 0.7
  ) +
  labs(x = "Sample Type", y = "SV Frequency") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1))
```

### Calculate Normalized SV Frequency Per Sample

To adjust the plot for the known batch effect, we next normalize every project 
to the value for sample_type 'HCT_C160_dox_0.4APH_M', sample_label 'M +APH', i.e.,
the sample expressing wild-type TTF2 with SV induction (if you want to change this,
edit `sample_type == "XXX"` below and re-knit this file).

```{r}
ref_freqs <- data[sample_type == "HCT_C160_dox_0.4APH_M", .(project, ref_sv_freq = sv_freq)]
ref_freqs
data <- merge(data, ref_freqs, by = c("project"), all.x = TRUE)
data[, norm_sv_freq := sv_freq / ref_sv_freq]
data[1:5, .(project, sample_group, sv_freq, ref_sv_freq, norm_sv_freq)]
```

### Calculate Mean Normalized SV Frequency Per Sample Type

```{r}
grouped_data <- data[, .(
  mean_sv_freq = mean(sv_freq),
  mean_norm_sv_freq = mean(norm_sv_freq)
), keyby = .(sample_group)]
grouped_data[1:5]
```

### Plot Normalized SV Frequency

```{r}
ggplot() +
  geom_col(
    data = grouped_data,
    aes(x = sample_group, y = mean_norm_sv_freq),
    fill = "grey80", color = "black", width = 0.7
  ) +
  geom_jitter(
    data = data,
    aes(x = sample_group, y = norm_sv_freq, color = project),
    width = 0.15, height = 0, size = 2, alpha = 0.7
  ) +
  labs(x = "Sample Type", y = "Normalized SV Frequency") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1))
```

### Calculate Intersample Difference Statistics - One-Sample t-Test, Normalized

As a first pass at assessing significance of the possible small effect, 
calculate the p-value of the three normalized SV frequency values for each 
sample type vs. the expected mean value of 1.0 (according to the null hypothesis)
using a one-sample t-test. 

```{r}
p_t1 <- data[, .(p_t1 = tryCatch(
  t.test(norm_sv_freq, mu = 1.0)$p.value, 
  error = function(e) NA_real_)
), by = .(sample_group)]
p_t1[, signif := ifelse(p_t1 < 0.05, "*", "")]
p_t1
```

### Calculate Intersample Difference Statistics - GLM with Project=Batch Parameter

This is how we calculated inter-sample significance in our 
[Nat Comm paper](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39505880/).
The method uses a generalized linear model based on the negative binomial 
distribution (appropriate for overdispersed counting statistics) including
parameter `project` to account for batch effects and offset(log_coverage)
to weight by the relative coverage depth of each sample.

The relevant methods section from the paper:

>To appropriately compare SV Frequency between experimental groups, e.g., wild type
vs. mutant, we performed  pairwise intergroup comparisons using a generalized linear
model based on the NBD in which the number of detected SVs, nSVs, varied as a function
of the experimental group and batch as independent covariates. Target region coverage
per sample was included as an offset parameter of slope 1 to effectively model 
SV Frequency. The relevant R language expression is 
‘fit = MASS::glm.nb(nSvs ~ group + batch + offset(log(coverage))‘, where 
‘group‘ and ‘batch‘ are categorical variables and the p-value of the intergroup 
comparison was obtained from the ‘group‘ variable as ‘coef(summary(fit))[2,4]‘. 
When glm.nb failed to return a result, the p-value was calculated using the glm 
function poisson model without overdispersion; such cases are denoted with a 
dashed significance line in plots. Throughout, we used p <= 0.01 as a significance 
threshold...

In practice for these TTF2 data, glm.nb routinely exceeded maximum iterations
and failed to converge, as happens if theta is very large, i.e., data are not 
that overdisperse. In that case, reverting to glm using quasipoisson gives more 
reliable results while still allowing for a theta factor and not a strict poisson.

```{r}
data[, log_coverage := log(coverage)]
sample_groups <- grouped_data$sample_group
p_glm <- do.call(rbind, lapply(sample_groups, function(group_1){
  do.call(rbind, lapply(sample_groups, function(group_2){
    if (group_1 == group_2) return(NULL) # require samples per non-identical group
    if (data[sample_group == group_1, .N] < 2) return(NULL)
    if (data[sample_group == group_2, .N] < 2) return(NULL)
    # fit <- glm.nb(
    #    deletion ~ sample_group + project + offset(log_coverage),
    #    data = data[sample_group %in% c(group_1, group_2)],
    #    control = glm.control(maxit = 100)
    # )
    fit <- glm(
        deletion ~ sample_group + project + offset(log_coverage),
        data = data[sample_group %in% c(group_1, group_2)],
        family = "quasipoisson"
    )
    data.table(group_1, group_2, p_glm = signif(coef(summary(fit))[2, 4], 3))
  }))
}))
p_glm[, signif := ifelse(p_glm < 0.05, "*", "")]
p_glm
```

Cast long to wide.

```{r}
dcast(p_glm, group_1 ~ group_2, value.var = "p_glm")
dcast(p_glm, group_1 ~ group_2, value.var = "signif")
```


### Calculate Intersample Difference Statistics – GLMM with Project as a Random Effect

The GLM analysis above accounts for batch effects by including project as a fixed effect. Because each svCapture sequencing run contains all experimental conditions, we additionally modeled batch as a random effect using a generalized linear mixed model (GLMM), while retaining an appropriate count-based model and normalization for sequencing depth via an offset of log(coverage).

GLMMs were fit using **glmmTMB**. A negative binomial distribution (nbinom2) was used by default to accommodate overdispersion. If the negative binomial model failed to converge or exhibited a non–positive-definite Hessian, an alternative negative binomial parameterization (nbinom1) was attempted; if this also failed, a Poisson GLMM was used as a last resort. Comparisons for which all models were unstable were reported as NA rather than assigning unreliable p-values.

For each pairwise comparison, factor levels were explicitly ordered so that estimated rate ratios represent the SV rate in the second group relative to the first group.

```{r}
library(glmmTMB)

# Ensure log coverage is available
if (!("log_coverage" %in% names(data))) data[, log_coverage := log(coverage)]

# Helper: only trust fits that converged AND have a positive-definite Hessian
is_ok <- function(fit) {
  if (is.null(fit)) return(FALSE)
  isTRUE(fit$fit$convergence == 0) && isTRUE(fit$sdr$pdHess)
}


# Control: give optimizer more room (helps small datasets / boundary fits)
ctrl <- glmmTMBControl(optCtrl = list(iter.max = 1e4, eval.max = 1e4))

sample_groups <- grouped_data$sample_group

p_glmm <- do.call(rbind, lapply(sample_groups, function(group_1){
  do.call(rbind, lapply(sample_groups, function(group_2){

    if (group_1 == group_2) return(NULL)
    if (data[sample_group == group_1, .N] < 2) return(NULL)
    if (data[sample_group == group_2, .N] < 2) return(NULL)

    dsub <- copy(data[sample_group %in% c(group_1, group_2)])
    dsub[, sample_group := factor(sample_group, levels = c(group_1, group_2))]

    # Try NB2 → NB1 → (last resort) Poisson
    fit_nb2 <- tryCatch(
      suppressWarnings(glmmTMB(
        deletion ~ sample_group + offset(log_coverage) + (1 | project),
        data = dsub,
        family = nbinom2(),
        control = ctrl
      )),
      error = function(e) NULL
    )

    nb2_ok <- is_ok(fit_nb2)
    fit <- fit_nb2
    used_family <- "nbinom2"
    note <- ""

    if (!nb2_ok) {
      fit_nb1 <- tryCatch(
        suppressWarnings(glmmTMB(
          deletion ~ sample_group + offset(log_coverage) + (1 | project),
          data = dsub,
          family = nbinom1(),
          control = ctrl
        )),
        error = function(e) NULL
      )

      nb1_ok <- is_ok(fit_nb1)
      fit <- fit_nb1
      used_family <- "nbinom1"
      note <- if (nb1_ok) "NB2_badfit_used_NB1" else "NB2_badfit_NB1_badfit"
    }

    if (!is_ok(fit)) {
      fit_pois <- tryCatch(
        suppressWarnings(glmmTMB(
          deletion ~ sample_group + offset(log_coverage) + (1 | project),
          data = dsub,
          family = poisson(),
          control = ctrl
        )),
        error = function(e) NULL
      )

      pois_ok <- is_ok(fit_pois)
      fit <- fit_pois
      used_family <- "poisson"
      note <- if (pois_ok) paste(note, "used_Poisson") else paste(note, "Poisson_badfit")
    }

    if (!is_ok(fit)) {
      return(data.table(
        group_1, group_2,
        p_glmm_wald = NA_real_,
        p_glmm_lrt  = NA_real_,
        rr = NA_real_,
        family = paste0(used_family, "_badfit"),
        nb_ok = nb2_ok,
        note = note
      ))
    }

    coefs <- summary(fit)$coefficients$cond
    term <- grep("^sample_group", rownames(coefs), value = TRUE)[1]

    p_wald <- coefs[term, "Pr(>|z|)"]
    beta   <- coefs[term, "Estimate"]
    rr_    <- exp(beta)

    # Likelihood-ratio test (often more stable than Wald in tiny N)
    p_lrt <- NA_real_
    fit0 <- tryCatch(update(fit, . ~ . - sample_group), error = function(e) NULL)
    if (!is.null(fit0) && is_ok(fit0)) {
      a <- tryCatch(anova(fit0, fit), error = function(e) NULL)
      if (!is.null(a) && nrow(a) >= 2 && "Pr(>Chisq)" %in% colnames(a)) {
        p_lrt <- a$`Pr(>Chisq)`[2]
      }
    }

    data.table(
      group_1, group_2,
      p_glmm_wald = signif(p_wald, 3),
      p_glmm_lrt  = signif(p_lrt,  3),
      rr = signif(rr_, 3),
      family = used_family,
      nb_ok = nb2_ok,
      note = note
    )
  }))
}))

p_glmm[, signif_wald := ifelse(!is.na(p_glmm_wald) & p_glmm_wald < 0.05, "*", "")]
p_glmm[, signif_lrt  := ifelse(!is.na(p_glmm_lrt)  & p_glmm_lrt  < 0.05, "*", "")]

```


Cast long to wide.

```{r}
dcast(p_glmm, group_1 ~ group_2, value.var = "p_glmm_wald")
dcast(p_glmm, group_1 ~ group_2, value.var = "signif_wald")

# Optional: LRT versions
dcast(p_glmm, group_1 ~ group_2, value.var = "p_glmm_lrt")
dcast(p_glmm, group_1 ~ group_2, value.var = "signif_lrt")
```


## "Conclusions"

Across multiple analytical frameworks, including GLMs and generalized linear mixed models (GLMMs) that account for sequencing depth via an offset and for batch effects via a random effect, the overall conclusions are broadly consistent. Effect sizes are modest, and statistical power is limited by sample size and technical variability.

Importantly, modeling batch as a random effect using a GLMM strengthens the evidence that SV frequency is reduced relative to M +APH in the degraded and degraded +K16A conditions. These differences reach statistical significance under the GLMM likelihood-ratio test, indicating that the observed reductions are robust to batch effects and coverage normalization.

In contrast, WT addback does not show a consistent or robust difference relative to M +APH, with significance depending on model choice and not supported across all analytical approaches. This suggests that WT addback largely restores SV frequency toward the M +APH baseline.

### Saving Output Tables

Writing output CSV files.

```{r}
write.csv(data,         "TTF2_Summary_012626.output.data.csv")
write.csv(grouped_data, "TTF2_Summary_012626.output.grouped_data.csv")
write.csv(p_t1,         "TTF2_Summary_012626.output.p_t1.csv")
write.csv(p_glm,        "TTF2_Summary_012626.output.p_glm.csv")
write.csv(p_glmm,       "TTF2_Summary_012626.output.p_glmm.csv")
```
